A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Learning Theory for Kernel Bilevel Optimization with the same authors and central theoretical results. All 36 pages of v1 and 47 pages of v2, including their appendices, support a reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports theoretical bounds and proofs, including Appendices A–G. Its application examples are mathematical formulations, without original experimental or data-analysis results.

after.justification: Section 5 and Appendix I report original synthetic instrumental-variable regression experiments. Figures 2 and 3 show empirical approximation errors and gradient-descent behavior.

M1.justification: The KBO framework, adjoint-based gradient estimator, and gradient and projected-gradient procedures are retained. Appendix I specializes these to a tractable experimental example; its random Fourier features approximate population reference quantities for evaluation.

E1.justification: v1 only formulates application examples. v2 introduces actual evaluation on synthetic instrumental-variable regression, using Gaussian instruments and Student’s t instruments with degrees of freedom 2.1, 2.5, and 2.9.

E2.justification: Neither version empirically evaluates competing algorithms. v2 compares behavior across data distributions and against a theoretical slope; cited instrumental-regression methods and Nyström approximations are not evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: v2 introduces an experimental protocol with sample sizes from 100 to 5,000, both equal and unequal inner/outer sizes, random initialization, backtracking gradient descent, and a gradient-norm stopping threshold of 10^-5. Population references use 1,000,000 samples and 26,000 random Fourier features. v1 has no corresponding experimental protocol.

E4.justification: v2 adds tests of sensitivity to instrument-distribution tails and an analysis of inner/outer sample imbalance. Appendix I.5 varies both sample sizes and displays their effects on approximation errors and stationarity in Figure 3. These analyses are absent from v1.

E5.justification: v2 introduces reporting over 50 runs, with means and 95% confidence intervals in Figure 2 and logarithms of 50-run means in Figure 3. v1 contains no empirical repeated-run or uncertainty reporting. The new reporting does not establish how randomness varies between runs.

E6.justification: Figure 2 adds empirical value-error, gradient-error, and stationarity curves that approximately follow the predicted inverse-square-root sample-size trend. Figure 3 adds the finding of lower errors near balanced inner/outer sample sizes. These are new empirical findings, with no earlier experimental scores to compare directly.

T1.justification: The main rates and proof framework remain intact. v2 adds Borel/measurability conditions and probabilistic/variance consequences, corrects the chain-rule sign, projected-gradient corollary, matrix-identity definition, and a U-statistic normalization factor. Appendix I adds specialized IVR and Fourier-feature derivations, without establishing a new generalization regime.

C1.justification: The central claims about uniform value/gradient bounds and equivalent gradient estimators remain. v2 adds empirical illustration to the abstract, explicitly positions its U-process technique as novel relative to finite-dimensional analyses, and adds a practical claim about balancing inner and outer sample sizes.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands the fixed-regularization bias, variance, and optimization tradeoff and explains obstacles to unregularized/minimax guarantees. Its conclusion treats stochastic extensions as an open challenge, replacing v1’s expectation of ready extension, and adds limitations concerning conservative constants and nonsmooth losses. The explicit Markovian-data/reinforcement-learning future direction is removed.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-access link, the synthetic data generator, hyperparameters, closed-form experimental estimators, and blockwise Fourier-feature computations. Appendix I.4 specifies JAX, an NVIDIA RTX 6000 ADA GPU, approximately 15 hours runtime, p=3, d=4, lambda=0.01, and kernel bandwidth 0.2. v1 lacks this experimental implementation information.

R1.justification: Section 3.1 and new Appendix A substantially expand comparisons with non-kernel stability bounds, sieve-based instrumental regression, and spectral/minimax theory. Added citations include Oymak et al., Arora et al., and Wang et al.’s stability lower bounds. The already-cited Meunier et al. work receives a substantive comparison explaining differences in objectives and regularization.

P1.justification: v2 extensively edits and expands the abstract, explanatory passages, and conclusion. The proof strategy moves from Section 5 to Section 4.2; gradient-descent proofs and the projected-gradient discussion move to Appendix E.4. New appendix organization and a contents list substantially change navigation and narrative structure.

P2.justification: The main text and references change from two columns to a single-column format, substantially reflowing equations and text. Figure 1 is retained with changed placement, while v2 adds the four-panel convergence plots in Figure 2 and four sample-size heatmaps in Figure 3.

improvement.justification: v2 improves precision through mathematical corrections, clearer research positioning, and explicit fixed-regularization limitations. Section 5 and Appendix I add documented empirical illustrations of the retained theory. Their additional validation is limited to one synthetic setting with approximate population references, and randomness across the 50 runs remains ambiguously described. The evidence supports a useful but limited overall quality gain.
